answers.Q1: A branch-local comment is not independent evidence: the same author can change the code, paste an expectation that matches it, and add “# confirmed”. proofdeck uses provenance from before the branch (or an approved, unchanged requirement/data source), because a comment can only assert confirmation, not establish it.
answers.Q2: proofdeck is a changed-line proof gate, not a mutation-testing leaderboard. It reports the actionable fact for each line—whether a behavior-changing mutant was noticed, merely run, never run, or only noticed through fakes—rather than an aggregate score that can hide an important unproved line or encourage score gaming.
answers.Q3: Default values occur on a function-definition statement. proofdeck classifies definitions as arid/non-mutation targets, so it mutates executable behavioral logic rather than declaration/signature lines; consequently no mutant is generated for a default argument value.
answers.Q4: An approved requirement is the pre-branch contract. Letting a branch edit its examples to match its new implementation would let the branch change code, test, and alleged specification together, laundering a wrong result into a passing proof. The changed requirement must therefore be reviewed as a contract change and fails the gate.
answers.Q5: It protects the fast fork/schemata execution mode while preserving trustworthy diagnostics. The user gets mutation checks whose switched code really has mutant behavior, while source line numbers still refer to the original file—so findings point to the correct changed line—without starting pytest once per mutant.
answers.Q6: Machine-readable report consumers—especially CI/review tooling and reviewers using its JSON—use this provenance to distinguish a line that was genuinely checked by a real test from one whose only killing tests replaced collaborators with fakes. They can also distinguish tests that merely ran a line from tests that actually noticed its mutation, and see which collaborators each test faked.

cat proofdeck/mutate.py; cat proofdeck/provenance.py; cat proofdeck/report.py
cat pyproject.toml; sed -n '100,220p' proofdeck/report.py; sed -n '100,220p' proofdeck/provenance.py; cat tests/conftest.py

answers.Q2: The project considers mutation scores and percentages neither concrete nor actionable. Instead it reports the specific changed path and line, together with the exact mutation that tests failed to notice, which gives a reviewer an actionable issue.
answers.Q3: Default argument values are classified as arid signature content. Mutating them produces reviewer-noise rather than useful findings; the requirements specifically note that default-argument mutants were the most-rejected Python mutants at Google.
answers.Q4: An approved requirement is evidence only because it existed on the base branch and was previously reviewed by a person. answers.Q1: A branch-written comment is self-attestation, not independent evidence: the same author/change can alter the code, paste its current output as the expectation, and add “# confirmed.” Confirmation must come from something that predates or is independent of the branch—such as an approved requirement, an existing assertion, or pre-existing test data—so that a wrong implementation cannot validate itself.
answers.Q2: Proofdeck is intentionally a changed-line proof gate, not a mutation-testing leaderboard. It reports the actionable fact at each changed line—whether a breaking mutation was noticed, merely ran, never ran, or was only noticed through fakes. An aggregate mutation score/percentage could obscure an important unproved line and encourages optimizing a denominator rather than demonstrating that each change is actually checked.
answers.Q3: Default argument values are deliberately classified as arid/noise on a function-definition line, rather than as executable logic to mutate. Proofdeck therefore does not generate mutants for them; its mutation targets are changed behavioral logic, not declaration/default-value syntax.
answers.Q4: Approved requirements are the independent contract against which the branch is meant to be checked. Allowing a branch to edit an existing example to match its implementation would let the implementation rewrite its own acceptance criteria. The project treats that as a requirement change requiring review/approval, and fails the gate so the change cannot silently ratify the code.
answers.Q5: It protects the user benefit of fast fork-mode mutation checking without sacrificing correctness or useful locations: users get code that behaves exactly as the selected mutant would behave, while findings still name the original source line. That enables one pytest start for many mutants while preserving trustworthy, line-accurate review output.
answers.Q6: This serves reviewers and machine consumers of the JSON report (for example CI/reporting integrations). They can see which tests executed and killed a line and which collaborators each test faked, letting them distinguish a genuinely checked line from one whose mutation was only noticed by a test that mocked/faked the relevant collaboration.

Letting the branch edit an existing requirement example to match its implementation would let an author rewrite the oracle and retroactively justify incorrect behavior. Such a change needs separate approval, so it fails the gate.
answers.Q5: It protects the user’s fast fork-mode experience: one pytest start can test many mutants, while each selected mutant still behaves exactly like a real source replacement. It also preserves original source line numbers, so coverage, findings, and displayed locations point to the user’s actual code lines.
answers.Q6: It serves machine/report consumers, especially CI integrations and reviewers consuming JSON. They can distinguish a line that a test merely ran from one whose mutation that test noticed, and distinguish real checking from a result obtained while collaborators were faked.

answers.Q1: Because a confirmation comment written on the branch is not independent evidence: the same author/agent that wrote potentially buggy code can also write “# confirmed.” proofdeck accepts only base-branch assertions/data or approved requirements as confirmation, and lists branch-written expectations—including correct tests and comments—as unconfirmed.
answers.Q2: Scores and percentages were found to be neither concrete nor actionable. proofdeck instead reports the actionable unit: the path and line containing a change that tests did not notice, along with the exact mutant/change.
answers.Q3: Default argument values are classified as arid signature syntax and are never mutated. Such mutants are noise that reviewers ignore; the requirements specifically note that mutating defaults was the most-rejected Python mutant at Google.
answers.Q4: An approved requirement must come from the base branch, where a person reviewed it. Allowing a branch to change its requirement example alongside its code would let the branch make the specification agree with buggy new output, defeating the independent check. Requirements therefore change in their own reviewed change, not together with the code judged against them.
answers.Q5: It protects the fork-mode schemata implementation. Users get the speed benefit of running pytest once while still receiving results equivalent to running each real mutant: switching a mutant changes runtime behavior exactly as that source mutation would, and source line numbers remain stable so findings point to the correct user-visible lines.
answers.Q6: It serves consumers that understand requirement intent, specifically specdeck-style tooling and reviewers of the JSON report. They can distinguish a line genuinely checked with real collaborators from one noticed only through fakes, and distinguish a requirement that is met by a real check from one that is only mock-proven or still unproven.
